source.title: Equifinality in Mixture of Experts: Routing Topology Does Not Determine Language Modeling Quality

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model losses across MoE routing and architecture variants and evaluates downstream-task performance against pretraining perplexity. It does not reproduce scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Chinchilla scaling and says it follows it to choose a training duration, but does not test a loss power law or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its own relevant results concern architecture/topology comparisons (V4) and whether pretraining-PPL ranking predicts downstream ranking (V6).
record.test_reason: The study compares converged validation loss across MoE routing-topology variants at a matched ~76–84M parameter count, which is a new setting for V4 (shape details at fixed parameters). It also checks whether pretraining-PPL ranking predicts zero-shot downstream ranking, which bears weakly on V6. It fits no power laws and does no compute-allocation sweep. It cites Chinchilla only to choose a training length.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but one wording needs correcting: the authors say pretraining-PPL ranking (not 'downstream PPL rankings') does not predict downstream benchmark ranking. Their core conclusion is that, within cosine-routed MoE at 76–138M params, routing topology does not determine converged language-modeling quality, and that routing capacity matters more than mechanism or topology. They make no claims about general scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation, and they explicitly do not claim generalisation to billion-parameter scale.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies MoE routing and topology comparisons rather than fitting loss-scaling laws or deriving a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that depth rankings differ between underfitting and convergence; it also reports results across routing topology, expert rank, and corpus. These are not sensitivity tests of scaling-law fitting choices.
record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and checkpoints will be released upon publication but gives no URL.
record.problems: The principal evidence is from relatively small models (76–138M parameters); the authors explicitly say generalization to billion-parameter models is untested. Downstream results are near chance, and exact benchmark breakdowns are deferred to supplementary logs.
record.rows_left_out: Other routing, halting, expert-ablation, and training-stage results were not extracted because they do not measure a version of the stated scaling-law claim. The linear-router and dense comparisons were also not included as V4 rows because they change routing mechanism or active computation rather than isolating architecture-detail effects at a matched parameter count.

untested.parts: No fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No compute-budget sweep or optimal N/D fit.
Dense transformer depth/width/heads variation; shapes over a wide range; other sizes. Only MoE routing topology at ~76–84M is tested.
No power law fitted in any modality or regime. The second corpus is text only, with no fit.
Downstream improvement with model scale; loss–accuracy relation across a meaningful loss range.
No exponent or fitting-choice sensitivity analysis.

missing.what: Underfitting-regime depth advantage: at 20K steps, Deep 136.70 vs Wide 149.80 PPL (8.8%) at 76M, which inverts to Wide better by 2.0% at convergence
Linear router (PPL 32.76, 1.17 PPL better than the best cosine variant) shows no downstream advantage
K×τ sparsity/temperature sweep: 10 configurations at fixed pool within 0.82 PPL

record.verdict_notes: Routing topology (hop count versus top-k width over shared experts) is only loosely the kind of 'shape' in V4, so the V4 link is a stretch; treat it as a new-setting test. The record's V4 limits_scope label was about untested breadth, so it was moved to untested. In its place, a text-based limits_scope cites training-stage dependence and the layer-count effect. The V6 evidence is weak because of near-chance accuracy, unreported per-model accuracies and tiny PPL differences, so it is labelled limits_scope rather than challenges. r12 and r13 were relinked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict much larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or fit of optimal parameter and token counts.
Only selected MoE routing/topology variants are compared, mostly around 76–84M parameters; this does not establish invariance across a wide range of model architectures or sizes.
No power-law test in other modalities or regimes. OpenWebText is a second text corpus, but the study does not fit a power law there.
Tests the relation between pretraining-PPL ranking and downstream accuracy for selected small MoE variants, not downstream scaling across model sizes.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation sensitivity to fitting choices. The underfitting-to-convergence change in topology ranking is not a test of a fitted scaling law.

rows.subject: ST-MoE Wide 1×12

rows.baseline: Other cosine-routing variants; equivalence margin δ = 1 PPL
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation 0.25 across 3 seeds; pairwise bootstrap CIs reported in Table 13
rows.note: The paper reports all five cosine variants equivalent within the stated 1-PPL margin, although some pairwise differences are statistically detectable.

rows.subject: ST-MoE Wide 1×4 rank-16
rows.stage_stated: converged; training duration not separately stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared Wide and Deep routing at rank-16 expert size.
rows.note: The paper says the two rank-16 topologies converge within 0.55 PPL and describes the comparison as supportive but not strictly controlled across ranks.
rows.check: The Wide–Deep gap at rank-16 is small (0.55 PPL). But this ~84M configuration uses 4 layers instead of 8 and lands about 3.5 PPL (~10%) worse than the rank-1 8-layer variants at a similar parameter count. That cross-configuration shape effect is not captured in the row.

rows.subject: ST-MoE Deep 2×2 rank-16
rows.stage_stated: converged; training duration not separately stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared Deep and Wide routing at rank-16 expert size.
rows.note: The paper attributes the higher absolute PPL to halved attention depth and says the topology gap is comparable to that in the rank-1 comparison.
rows.check: Same as r6. The authors attribute the higher absolute PPL to halved attention depth, a shape change at roughly fixed parameters that moves loss far more than topology does.

rows.subject: ST-MoE Wide 1×12
rows.stage_stated: converged; OpenWebText training duration not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared Wide and Deep routing on a second text corpus.
rows.baseline: ST-MoE Deep 3×4; Wide–Deep mean gap reported as 0.03 PPL
rows.note: The paper reports a 0.03-PPL difference between the Wide and Deep means across six total runs.

rows.subject: ST-MoE Deep 3×4
rows.stage_stated: converged; OpenWebText training duration not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared Deep and Wide routing on a second text corpus.
rows.baseline: ST-MoE Wide 1×12; Wide–Deep mean gap reported as 0.03 PPL
rows.note: The paper reports that the gap is 6× smaller than seed noise.

rows.subject: Wide 1×12 versus Deep 3×4 and Magnitude Hack
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream accuracy ranking with pretraining-PPL ranking.
rows.measure: Zero-shot accuracy and its relation to pretraining PPL
rows.baseline: Deep 3×4 and Magnitude Hack; Wide has best PPL
rows.value: Wide is the worst downstream performer on HellaSwag versus both Deep and Magnitude Hack (p < 0.01); only the Deep–Magnitude Hack pair passes TOST equivalence at δ = 0.02
rows.uncertainty: McNemar p < 0.01 for Wide versus both other variants; TOST result stated for one of nine variant–benchmark pairs
rows.note: The authors state that PPL ranking does not predict downstream ranking. Exact per-model accuracies are referred to supplementary logs and are not given in the paper text.
rows.check: This is a ranking reversal among models whose PPL differs by under 1 PPL, with accuracies near chance. Per-model accuracies are not given, so the magnitude can't be read.

rows.note: The authors state that PPL ranking does not predict downstream ranking. Exact per-model accuracies are not given in the paper text.

relationships.condition: Converged (50K steps, 1.64B tokens) cosine-routed MoE topology variants at ~76–84M params, on WikiText-103 and OpenWebText, at rank-1 and rank-16
relationships.reason: Five topology variants fall within a 0.79 PPL band (TOST equivalence at 1 PPL); Wide–Deep gaps are 0.55 PPL at rank-16 and 0.03 PPL on OpenWebText (r1–r9).
relationships.display_finding: Five WikiText-103 topology variants occupied a 0.79-perplexity band and met a 1-perplexity equivalence margin; wide–deep gaps were 0.55 at rank 16 and 0.03 on OpenWebText.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Converged (50K steps, 1.64B tokens) cosine-routed MoE topology variants at ~76–84M params, on WikiText-103 and OpenWebText, at rank-1 and rank-16
source_check.reason: The support label is justified by the reported small topology gaps, but the condition needs separate training-duration descriptions for WikiText-103 and OpenWebText. Section 8.2 reports approximately 6.5 OpenWebText epochs over 507M corpus tokens, inconsistent with applying 1.64B tokens uniformly. The formal five-variant TOST result concerns the primary WikiText-103 comparison.

relationships.condition: Undertrained regime (5–20K steps), and the rank-16 4-layer configuration versus rank-1 8-layer configurations at ~84M params
relationships.reason: From the text, not the rows: at 20K steps Deep beats Wide by 8.8% PPL. The 4-layer rank-16 models sit ~10% higher PPL than the 8-layer rank-1 models at similar parameter count (r6, r7 vs r1). So shape effects depend on training stage and on layer count.
relationships.display_finding: At 20K steps, Deep had 8.8% lower perplexity than Wide; four-layer rank-16 models had about 10% higher perplexity than similarly sized eight-layer rank-1 models.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Undertrained regime (5–20K steps), and the rank-16 4-layer configuration versus rank-1 8-layer configurations at ~84M params
source_check.reason: Appendix C and Table 17 report an 8.8% undertrained Deep advantage. Section 8.1 reports higher absolute perplexity for four-layer rank-16 configurations at a similar parameter budget and attributes it to reduced attention depth; several architectural factors change across ranks.

relationships.condition: Three cosine variants at 76–84M with near-equal PPL; zero-shot HellaSwag and ARC-Easy near chance
relationships.reason: The best-PPL variant (Wide) is the worst downstream (p<0.01), and the linear router's 1.2-PPL lead gives no downstream gain. With under-1-PPL differences at near-chance accuracy, this limits rather than refutes loss-based predictability (r10, r11).
relationships.display_finding: Wide had the best perplexity but significantly worse downstream accuracy than the other cosine variants (p<0.01), while the linear router's 1.2-point perplexity advantage yielded no downstream gain.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Three cosine variants at 76–84M with near-equal PPL; zero-shot HellaSwag and ARC-Easy near chance
source_check.reason: Within this condition, Section 4.4 explicitly reports reversed loss-based ranking: Wide has the best perplexity but significantly worse HellaSwag and ARC-Easy accuracy than Deep and Magnitude Hack. The linear router's lower perplexity yields no downstream advantage. Under the verdict rules, absent or reversed improvement challenges the loss-based branch of V6; near-chance performance limits the strength and scope of that evidence. Scale-based predictability remains untested.

relation.reason: The study directly measures validation perplexity across architectural variants at comparable parameter budgets and compares perplexity rankings with downstream rankings.

tranche.reason: Matched-parameter MoE routing-topology comparisons provide a new architectural setting with results on V4.

source_check.notes: The equivalence margin is 0.03 cross-entropy loss, approximately 1 PPL. Appendix B.5 claims all bootstrap intervals remain within that margin while listing a block-bootstrap lower bound of −0.031, an internal inconsistency.

statements.correction: WikiText-103: 50K steps, 1.64B tokens; five cosine variants, 15 runs, range 33.93–34.72 PPL. OpenWebText: Wide 34.25 ± 0.20, Deep 34.22 ± 0.02, three seeds each; approximately 6.5 epochs over 507M corpus tokens; training-duration reporting inconsistent with the general marathon configuration.
statements.problem: The 0.79-PPL band and 0.03-PPL OpenWebText gap are correct. The shared training-duration condition obscures inconsistent reporting: Section 8.2 describes OpenWebText as approximately 6.5 epochs over 507M tokens, whereas the marathon configuration specifies 50K steps and 1.64B tokens.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Five cosine-routing variants at 76–84M parameters on WikiText-103, and Wide–Deep rank-16 and OpenWebText comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Reported topology-related PPL differences are within 1 PPL for the five main variants; rank-16 and OpenWebText comparisons also show small Wide–Deep gaps (r1–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The tested ST-MoE configurations and model sizes in this paper
reader_labels.reason: The comparisons cover a restricted set of cosine-routed MoE variants and do not establish that architecture details matter little across a wide range of architectures or scales (r1–r9).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Pretraining-PPL versus zero-shot accuracy for the tested cosine variants on HellaSwag and ARC-Easy
reader_labels.reason: Wide has the best PPL but is reported as the worst downstream performer on both benchmarks, contrary to the tested PPL-ranking predictability (r10–r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All tested models at 76–84M parameters on the reported downstream benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: The authors caution that performance is near chance, limiting how strongly these evaluations can discriminate downstream predictability (r12–r13).
